facts.fact_text: The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the City of Sunderland College's proposal to build on the Arena.

The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to persuade the Council not to grant the City of Sunderland College permission to build on the Arena.
On or around 14 March 1998, the first applicant, together with her husband and son, set up two stands at the entrance of the shopping mall in the Galleries.
The stands set up by the first applicant on or around 14 March 1998 displayed posters alerting the public to the likely loss of the open space known as the Arena.
The stands set up by the first applicant on or around 14 March 1998 were used to seek signatures to present to the Council on behalf of Washington First Forum.
Security guards employed by Postel Properties Limited would not let the first applicant or her assistants continue to collect signatures on any land or premises owned by Postel Properties Limited.
The applicants had to remove their stands from the Galleries.
The applicants had to stop collecting signatures at the Galleries.
The fourth applicant continued to try to reach the public by setting up stands by the roadside on public footpaths.
The fourth applicant continued to try to reach the public by going to the old town centre at Concord.

In April 1998, the manager of one of the hypermarkets in the Galleries did not grant the applicants permission to collect signatures for a further petition.
In his reply of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries refused the third applicant access to the Galleries and adjacent car parks.

In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that he was obliged to refuse permission for Washington First Forum to carry out a petition within the Galleries or the adjacent car parks.
At common law, a private property owner may in certain circumstances be presumed to have extended an implied invitation to members of the public to come onto his land for lawful purposes.
At common law, the implied invitation to members of the public to enter private property applies to commercial premises such as shops, theatres and restaurants.
At common law, there is a presumption that a house owner authorises people to come up the path to his front door to deliver letters or newspapers or for political canvassing.
At common law, any implied invitation to members of the public to enter private property may be revoked at will.
At common law, a private person's ability to eject people from his land is generally unfettered and he does not have to justify his conduct or comply with any test of reasonableness.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), the applicants were young men who were barred from a shopping centre in Wellingborough by the private company owner CIN Properties Ltd on the basis that their behaviour was a nuisance.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), the Court of Appeal held that CIN Properties Ltd had the right to determine any licence which the applicants might have had to enter the shopping centre in Wellingborough.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips found that the local authority had not entered into any walkways agreement with CIN Properties Ltd within the meaning of section 18(1) of the Highways Act 1971 (later replaced by section 35 of the Highways Act 1980) which would have dedicated the walkways or footpaths as public rights of way.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips found that a walkways agreement within the meaning of section 18(1) of the Highways Act 1971 would have given the local council the power to issue by-laws regulating the use of those rights of way.
In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips found there was no basis for finding an equitable licence in favour of the applicants.
In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips considered case-law from North America concerning the applicants' arguments for the finding of some kind of public right.

In Uston v. Resorts International Inc. (1982) N.J. 445A.2d 370, the Supreme Court of New Jersey laid down as a general proposition that when property owners open their premises to the general public in pursuit of their own property interests, they have no right to exclude people unreasonably but have a duty not to act in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner towards persons who come on their premises.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips noted that the decision in Uston v. Resorts International Inc. (1982) N.J. 445A.2d 370 was based upon a previous decision of the Supreme Court of New Jersey in State v. Schmid (1980) N.J. 423A 2d 615, which clearly turned upon the constitutional freedoms of the First Amendment to the United States Federal Constitution.
In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips stated that the general proposition from Uston v. Resorts International Inc. has no application in English law.

In Harrison v. Carswell (1975) 62 D.L.R. 3d 68, the Supreme Court of Canada considered the right of an employee of a tenant in a shopping centre to picket her employer in the centre against the wishes of the owner of the centre.

In Harrison v. Carswell (1975) 62 D.L.R. 3d 68, the majority of the Supreme Court of Canada held that the employee had no right to picket her employer in the shopping centre and that the owner of the centre had sufficient control or possession of the common areas to enable it to invoke the remedy of trespass.

In Harrison v. Carswell (1975) 62 D.L.R. 3d 68, Laskin C.J.C. in a strong dissenting judgment held that since a shopping centre was freely accessible to the public, the public did not enter under a revocable licence subject only to the owner's whim.

In his dissenting judgment in Harrison v. Carswell (1975) 62 D.L.R. 3d 68, Laskin C.J.C. stated that members of the public visiting a shopping centre are privileged visitors whose privilege is revocable only upon misbehaviour or by reason of unlawful activity.
In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips accepted that courts may have to be ready to adapt the law to new social facts where necessary.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips held that there was no necessity for courts to adapt the law where Parliament had already made adequate provision for the new social facts in question, as it had by section 18 of the Highways Act 1971 and section 35 of the Highways Act 1980.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips held that where Parliament has legislated and the Council, as representing the public, chooses not to invoke the statutory machinery, it is not for the courts to intervene.

In CIN Properties Ltd v. Rawlins ([1995] 2 EGLR 130), Lord Phillips allowed the appeal on the basis that CIN Properties Ltd had the right, subject only to the issue under section 20 of the Race Relations Act 1976, to determine any licence the applicants may have had to enter the shopping centre.
In March 1998, the manager of one of the hypermarkets in the Galleries gave the applicants permission to set up stands within that store.
The permission granted by the manager of one of the hypermarkets in March 1998 allowed the applicants to transmit their message and to collect signatures, albeit from a reduced number of people.
In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that the Galleries is unique in that although it is the Town Centre, it is also privately owned.

In his letter of 14 April 1998, the manager of the Galleries stated that the owner's stance on all political and religious issues is one of strict neutrality and that he was charged with applying this philosophy.
The old town centre at Concord is visited by a much smaller number of Washington residents than the Galleries.
The fourth applicant produced a list of associations and others which were given permission to carry out collections, set up stands and displays within the Galleries.
The Salvation Army was given permission to carry out a collection before Christmas within the Galleries.
Local school choirs were given permission to carry out carol-singing and a collection before Christmas within the Galleries.
The Stop Smoking Campaign was given permission to set up an advertising display and hand out nicotine patches within the Galleries.
The Blood Transfusion Service was given permission to carry out a blood collection within the Galleries.
The Royal British Legion was given permission to carry out a collection for Armistice Day within the Galleries.
Various photographers were given permission to carry out advertising and taking of photographs within the Galleries.
British Gas was given permission to set up a staffed advertising display within the Galleries.
From 31 January to 6 March 2001, Sunderland Council ran a consultation campaign under the banner 'Your Council, Your Choice'.
The 'Your Council, Your Choice' campaign informed local residents of three leadership choices for the future of Sunderland Council.
Sunderland Council was allowed to use the Galleries for the 'Your Council, Your Choice' consultation campaign.
The 'Your Council, Your Choice' campaign was a statutory consultation exercise carried out under section 25 of the Local Government Act 2000.

Section 25 of the Local Government Act 2000 required local authorities to draw up proposals for the operation of 'executive arrangements' and consult local electors before sending them to the Secretary of State.
Some 8,500 people were reported as having responded to the 'Your Council, Your Choice' survey.

The Galleries was originally built by the Washington Development Corporation ('the Corporation'), a body set up by the government of the United Kingdom pursuant to an Act of Parliament to build the 'new' centre.
Public services were available in the vicinity of the Galleries.
The freehold of the careers' office within or near the Galleries was owned by the Council.
The freehold of the public library within or near the Galleries was owned by the Council.
The social services office within or near the Galleries was leased to the Council by the Secretary of State.
The health centre within or near the Galleries was leased to the Council by the Secretary of State.
The freehold of the police station within or near the Galleries was held on behalf of Northumbria Police Authority.
There was a post office within the Galleries.
The offices of the housing department within the Galleries were leased to the Council by Postel Properties Limited.
